cells.tense: The deciding is happening now, and it is yours while it happens.
cells.ask: Take one finished thing and say what it adds up to, then hand it on to someone, and notice what settles when you do.
cells.core:
You're holding the pen right now, and the draft is coming out clean. What arrives as a decision arrives whole — no arguing with it afterward, no circling back to check. The understanding underneath is total enough that the next move is obvious, and you keep moving because there's nothing to second-guess.

The quieter half of this is the one worth noticing. You're comfortable not having the answer yet when you don't. Nothing lands as a threat, so you can wait for the shape to show itself. That's what makes the speed safe — the fast part rides on the unhurried part. Someone near you benefits from that without knowing why. Say what the finished thing adds up to, pass it on, and let the next start find you empty-handed.
cells.sheetLine: You move with a clarity that doesn't need to announce itself.
cells.verb: moving with a clarity that needs no announcement
cells.place: the moment when things come together and are ready to be let go

cells.tense: You are already standing in the room where this has to work, before it has been built.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you are calling done, name exactly what still has to happen for it, and do the first small piece of that today.
cells.core:
You're deciding ahead of the thing itself. The plan is complete in your head — every branch mapped, every objection answered — and you're already braced for the moment it has to hold up. Some of that is real strength. Some of it is you carrying weight that hasn't been handed to you yet, and that part is costing you the ease the clarity is supposed to bring.

The bend is in the timing. You're treating things as finished so you can stop feeling like they might not be, and the bracing spreads until it's the thing you notice instead of the work. Go back and tell the truth about one thing that's still open. Do the next real step — not the whole sequence, just the piece in front of you. The structure holds better when you're not holding it from the future. "Everything's handled" can mean there's no room left for anyone else to be in it with you.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.ask: Name one thing that is genuinely finished, tell one person it's done, and leave it alone for a week.
cells.core:
The clarity is there — you can feel it when the question is clean — but it isn't reaching your hands. Something got decided once, or almost did, and the hesitation that started there now sits on top of decisions that have nothing to do with it. You wait for a certainty that already came and went, and the waiting looks like patience from the outside.

Things don't finish. They trail off, or they stay open in your head long after other people have moved on, and the not-finishing is a quiet kind of drain. One finished thing, named out loud to somebody, breaks the pattern faster than thinking about it will. Say it and stop working on it. What's done has been holding the whole time. What you're looking for is the part that's yours to lay down, not the part that's still coming. Some of what looks unfinished is just waiting for you to call it done and see what opens after.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's finished. You haven't let it be finished.

cells.tense: The pen is down and the page is already covered, because you have been writing without saying so.
cells.ask: Pick one thing people treat as settled, say out loud that you settled it, and let the saying be the whole action.
cells.core:
You're the one holding this together — the pace, the order, what counts as done — and you talk about it like it's just how things are. Nothing in you feels like command. It feels like noticing, or like doing the obvious next thing, and other people organize around that without anyone naming why.

What's absent is your claim on it. Saying so once changes what you're allowed to do next, and it also changes how your own effort lands when you look back at it. Pick one arrangement and say that you set it. "Let's run it this way" is different from naming what you already decided. It doesn't need defending, and it doesn't stop being true if it's acknowledged. You lose nothing by marking it, and you get the record straight.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering this and calling it just how things are.
